sections.title: Third week of development — gastrulation & neurulation

blocks.x: Human development begins with fertilization — the union of a spermatozoon and a secondary oocyte in the ampulla of the uterine tube — and proceeds through cleavage, blastocyst formation, implantation, and the establishment of all three germ layers by the end of the third week.

blocks.cap: Structure of a mature human spermatozoon, labelled head, mid-piece, tail, and end-piece

items: Fertilization — sperm penetrates the corona radiata, zona pellucida, and oocyte membrane, restoring the diploid number and forming the zygote
Cleavage — mitotic divisions of the zygote into blastomeres, forming the morula, then the blastocyst
Week 2 — implantation completes; the bilaminar germ disc (epiblast + hypoblast) forms
Week 3 — gastrulation converts the bilaminar disc into a trilaminar disc (ectoderm, mesoderm, endoderm); neurulation begins

blocks.x: These three weeks compress an extraordinary amount of decision-making: which sperm fertilizes the egg, whether one embryo becomes two (twinning), where implantation occurs, and how a simple two-layered disc organizes into the axes and germ layers that will build every organ system. Many of the most serious human birth defects trace back to errors introduced in exactly this window — often before a woman even knows she is pregnant.
How this module is organised
The sperm's journey, capacitation, and the three phases of fertilization.
Blastomere division, blastocyst formation, twinning, implantation, and the bilaminar disc.
Gastrulation, the notochord, neurulation, and the developing placenta and fetal membranes.

Fertilization occurs when a spermatozoon penetrates the corona radiata and zona pellucida and pierces the plasma membrane of a secondary oocyte, usually within the ampulla of the oviduct. Only about 1% of sperm deposited in the vagina enter the cervix, and spermatozoa may remain viable in the female tract for about 5 days.

blocks.cap: Diagram of the acrosome intact versus acrosome reacted, showing loss of the outer acrosomal membrane and plasma membrane
Diagram of ZP1, ZP2, ZP3 layers of the zona pellucida showing sperm binding, penetration, gamete fusion, cortical granule exocytosis, and the block to polyspermy

blocks.x: The trip toward the ampulla

Sperm movement is driven by muscular contractions of the uterus and uterine tubes, plus their own propulsion. The trip from cervix to oviduct takes a minimum of 2–7 hours. After reaching the isthmus, sperm become less motile and pause their migration.

At ovulation, sperm become motile again due to chemoattractants from the cumulus cells, swimming to the ampulla. Thermotaxis — sperm are guided by temperature through most of the tube (the tube containing the ovulated oocyte is slightly warmer), then navigate by the egg's chemical signal once close to the fertilization site.
Pre-fertilization: 3 required changes

A period of conditioning within the female tract (uterine tubes), lasting about 7 hours. Involves epithelial interactions between sperm and the tubal mucosa. The glycoprotein coat and seminal plasma proteins are removed from the plasma membrane surrounding the acrosomal region. Only capacitated sperm can pass through the corona radiata to undergo the acrosome reaction.
The ability of the spermatozoon to swim faster and more vigorously, making penetration of the zona pellucida easier once it contacts the oocyte.

Occurs after the sperm binds to the zona pellucida of the secondary oocyte, induced by zona proteins. Results in release of enzymes needed to penetrate the zona pellucida — acrosin and trypsin-like substances.
Fertilization — 3 phases

Of the 200–300 million sperm deposited in the vagina, only 300–500 reach the ampulla, and only one fertilizes the oocyte. The remaining sperm aid the fertilizing sperm by helping to break down the corona radiata and zona pellucida. Only capacitated sperm pass freely through the corona radiata cells.

The zona pellucida is a glycoprotein shell that facilitates and maintains sperm binding and induces the acrosomal reaction. ZP3 facilitates both binding and the acrosomal reaction. Release of acrosin allows the sperm to penetrate the zona and contact the oocyte's plasma membrane.

Initial adhesion is partly mediated by integrins on the oocyte and their ligands, disintegrins, on the sperm. Membrane fusion occurs via fertilin (an integral protein in the spermatozoon membrane) interacting with CD9 molecules and integrins on the oocyte's plasmalemma. Both the head and tail of the spermatozoon enter the oocyte cytoplasm, but the sperm's plasma membrane is left behind on the oocyte surface.
The zona pellucida

A glycoprotein covering of the primary oocyte, composed of four glycoproteins: ZP1 cross-links ZP2 with ZP3, preventing additional sperm binding; ZP2 acts as a secondary spermatozoa-binding protein; ZP3 permits sperm binding and facilitates the acrosome reaction; ZP4's function is unknown. After fertilization, the ovum secretes ovastacin, an enzyme that degrades ZP2, preventing additional sperm from binding.
Post-fertilization: the oocyte's 3 responses

Release of lysosomal enzymes from cortical granules makes the oocyte membrane impenetrable to other sperm, while the zona pellucida alters its structure/composition to prevent further sperm binding and penetration. Together these reactions prevent polyspermy.

The oocyte completes its second meiotic division immediately upon sperm entry (now called an ovum). One daughter cell — the polar body — receives very little cytoplasm; the other, the definitive oocyte, has chromosomes (22 + X) that arrange into a vesicular nucleus, the female pronucleus.

The sperm nucleus swells to form the male pronucleus, lying close to the female pronucleus; the sperm tail detaches and degenerates. The two pronuclei come into close contact, lose their nuclear envelopes, and their chromosomes intermingle to form a diploid zygote.

After the chromosomes intermingle, the centrosome contributed by the spermatozoon forms a mitotic spindle, and the zygote undergoes its first mitotic division, producing the first two blastomeres of the new embryo. All centrosomes of the new individual derive from the father; all mitochondria derive from the mother.
Results of fertilization
Half the chromosomes from the father, half from the mother — the zygote carries a new combination distinct from either parent.
An X-carrying sperm produces a female (XX); a Y-carrying sperm produces a male (XY). Chromosomal sex is fixed at fertilization.
Without fertilization, the oocyte usually degenerates about 24 hours after ovulation.

Cleavage is a series of mitotic divisions by which the large zygote is fractionated into numerous "normal size" cells. Each daughter cell is called a blastomere. Cleavage begins with the zygote, progresses through compaction to the morula stage, and terminates at the start of the blastocyst stage.

Labelled diagram of the blastocyst showing the embryonic pole, inner cell mass (embryoblast), blastocoel, outer cell mass (trophoblast), and abembryonic pole
Schematic diagram of the eight main types of conjoined twins: cephalopagus, thoracopagus, omphalopagus, ischiopagus, parapagus, craniopagus, pygopagus, and rachipagus

items: Individual blastomeres do not grow — cell size is reduced by almost half at each division
The final mass of cells is the same total size and genetic composition as the zygote
The first cleavage division occurs 1–5 days following ovulation; thereafter cells divide about once every 12 hours
As many as 8 generations of mitoses may occur without intervening cytoplasmic growth

blocks.x: Compaction & the morula

Until the 8-cell stage, blastomeres form a loosely arranged clump. After the 3rd cleavage, blastomeres maximize contact with each other, forming a compact ball held together by tight junctions — compaction. This process differentiates blastomeres into inner and outer cells with different fates.

Approximately 3 days after fertilization, the compacted embryo divides again to form a 16-cell morula (mulberry). Inner cells form the inner cell mass (embryoblast), and surrounding cells form the outer cell mass. The inner cell mass gives rise to tissues of the embryo proper; the outer cell mass forms the trophoblast, which later contributes to the placenta.
Blastocyst formation

As the morula enters the uterine cavity, fluid from the uterine tube penetrates through the zona pellucida into intercellular spaces of the inner cell mass. These spaces gradually become confluent, and a single cavity — the blastocoel — forms. At this point the embryo is a blastocyst.
Cells of the inner cell mass (embryoblast) collect at one pole; cells of the outer cell mass (trophoblast) flatten and form the epithelial wall of the blastocyst.

This allows implantation to begin. The blastocyst becomes surrounded by an inner cellular layer, the cytotrophoblast, and an outer multinucleated layer, the syncytiotrophoblast. L-selectin (CD62L) on trophoblast cells and its carbohydrate receptors on the uterine epithelium mediate initial attachment.
Twinning
Two offspring resulting from the same pregnancy, usually born in close succession; they can be the same or different sex.

c: 1 oocyte fertilized by a single spermatozoon
May share a placenta (monochorionic) or have separate placentas (dichorionic)

blocks.x: Monozygotic twins develop when one fertilized egg's zygote divides into two separate identical cells (embryos) at the first cleavage division — each part then develops into a baby.
Kinds of monozygotic twins

items: Zygote divides into two separate cells at the first cleavage division
Two inner cell masses develop, each giving rise to a separate embryo
A single inner cell mass forms but later divides, giving rise to two embryos
A single inner cell mass forms, divides incompletely, and Siamese (conjoined) twins result

blocks.x: Family history, maternal age >30 (rising FSH), race (higher in African-American women), obesity (BMI>30, raised estrogen), greater maternal height, breastfeeding during conception, high dairy intake (IGF), and reproductive technologies (ovulation-stimulating drugs, IVF).
Conjoined (Siamese) twins

Occurs in about 1 in 100,000 pregnancies ("pagus" = fixed or united). Two proposed causes: (1) identical twins normally develop 8–12 days after fertilization — if the embryo splits later (usually 13–15 days), separation stops before completion, producing conjoined twins; or (2) two separate embryos fuse together in early development. Conjoined twins are likely born premature, and one or both may be stillborn or die shortly after birth.

c: Joined side by side at the lower body
Two heads side by side on one torso (rare)
Joined at the back of the head/upper body, bottoms separate
Joined by part of the skull only; may share brain tissue
United at the thorax; heart always involved
United at the abdomen; 4 arms/4 legs; may share liver/GI/GU structures
Fused from upper chest to abdomen; usually share a heart
Joined at the lower spine, end-to-end at 180°; 4 arms, 2–4 legs, 1 set of genitalia
Joined back-to-back above the lumbar spine

items: Implantation completes
Trophoblast gives rise to 2 tissues: cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast
Embryoblast splits into 2 layers: epiblast and hypoblast
Two yolk sacs form: first the primary, then the secondary
Two new cavities form: the amniotic cavity and the chorionic cavity
Extraembryonic mesoderm develops and splits into somatic and splanchnic layers
Primitive uteroplacental circulation forms
The connecting stalk and prechordal plate form

blocks.x: Day-by-day progression

The blastocyst is partially embedded in the endometrial stroma. The trophoblast differentiates into the cytotrophoblast (inner mononucleated layer) and syncytiotrophoblast (outer multinucleated zone, no distinct cell boundaries). Mitotic figures occur only in the cytotrophoblast, whose cells migrate into and fuse with the syncytiotrophoblast. The embryoblast splits into hypoblast (small cuboidal cells adjacent to the blastocyst cavity) and epiblast (high columnar cells adjacent to the amniotic cavity) — together forming a flat, bilaminar disc. A small cavity within the epiblast enlarges to become the amniotic cavity.

blocks.cap: Labelled diagram of a 9-day human blastocyst showing trophoblastic lacunae, syncytiotrophoblast, cytotrophoblast, amniotic cavity, epiblast, hypoblast, exocoelomic membrane, and fibrin coagulum

blocks.x: The blastocyst is more deeply embedded; the surface defect is closed by a fibrin coagulum. At the embryonic pole, vacuoles appear in the syncytium and fuse to form large lacunae (the lacunar stage). At the abembryonic pole, flattened hypoblast-derived cells form the exocoelomic (Heuser's) membrane, which together with the hypoblast lines the exocoelomic cavity (primitive yolk sac).

The blastocyst is completely embedded; it produces a slight protrusion into the uterine lumen. Syncytiotrophoblast cells erode maternal capillaries (now called sinusoids); syncytial lacunae become continuous with sinusoids, and maternal blood enters the lacunar system, establishing uteroplacental circulation. A new epiblast-derived cell population forms loose connective tissue — extraembryonic mesoderm — filling the space around the amnion and yolk sac. Large cavities within it become confluent, forming the extraembryonic coelom (chorionic cavity).

The surface defect has usually healed (bleeding here can be mistaken for menstruation near day 28, causing errors in delivery-date estimation). Cytotrophoblast cells proliferate into the syncytiotrophoblast, forming primary villi. The hypoblast produces cells that form the secondary (definitive) yolk sac, smaller than the primitive yolk sac; portions of the primary yolk sac are pinched off as exocoelomic cysts. The extraembryonic mesoderm lining the cytotrophoblast becomes the chorionic plate; the connecting stalk (traversed by extraembryonic mesoderm) later becomes the umbilical cord.
Extraembryonic mesoderm layers

Growth of the bilaminar disc is slow compared to the trophoblast, remaining only 0.1–0.2 mm. Endometrial changes around the implantation site — polyhedral, glycogen/lipid-laden cells and edematous, extravasate-filled intercellular spaces — are called the decidua reaction, initially local, then spreading through the endometrium.
Clinical correlates — abnormal implantation

The syncytiotrophoblast produces hormones including hCG; by the end of week 2, hCG levels are sufficient for radioimmunoassay-based pregnancy testing. Since 50% of the embryo's genome is paternal, immunosuppressive cytokines/proteins and an unusual MHC class IB molecule (HLA-G) block recognition of the conceptus as foreign. Maternal autoimmune disease (e.g., lupus) may generate antibodies that attack and reject the conceptus.

If the blastocyst implants close to the internal cervical os, the placenta may later bridge the opening (placenta previa), risking severe bleeding. Implantation outside the uterus is an ectopic pregnancy — 95% occur in the uterine tube (mostly the ampulla); others occur in the ovary, or attach to the peritoneal lining of the rectouterine pouch (of Douglas), intestine, or omentum. Most ectopic embryos die around the second month, causing hemorrhage and abdominal pain.

Reproductive failure is common: even in fertile women, ~15% of oocytes are never fertilized; of fertilized eggs, 10–15% fail to implant; of those that implant, only 58% survive to the second week (16% of these are abnormal). By the time a first missed period occurs, only about 42% of eggs originally exposed to sperm are still surviving.

sections.title: Third week of development — gastrulation & neurulation

blocks.x: Gastrulation is the process by which the early embryo is transformed into a body with multiple cell and tissue types — it marks the commencement of the embryonic period (weeks 3–8) and transforms the bilaminar disc into a trilaminar one. The embryo is now called a gastrula.

blocks.cap: Three-dimensional diagram of the gastrulating embryonic disc showing Hensen's node, the primitive streak, epiblast, migrating cells, mesoderm, and endoderm displacing the endoblast
Transverse section through the trilaminar embryo showing amnioblasts, epiblast, intraembryonic and extraembryonic mesoderm, endoderm, and the hypoblast being displaced laterally

Diagram of neurulation showing the neural plate, neural plate border, neural folds converging over the neural groove, and the neural tube forming with neural crest cells breaking away on either side beneath the epidermis

blocks.x: The primitive streak & node

Gastrulation begins with formation of the primitive (Spemann's) streak — a narrow groove on the surface of the epiblast. The cranial end expands as the primitive (Hensen's) node, containing a circular depression, the primitive pit, continuous caudally with the primitive groove.

Formation of the primitive streak defines all major body axes: cranial-caudal, dorsal-ventral, medial-lateral, and left-right. At this stage, the embryo is pear-shaped, with a broader anterior end and narrower posterior end.
Formation of the germ layers

Epiblast cells migrate toward the primitive streak; on arrival they become flask-shaped, detach from the epiblast, and slip beneath it (invagination). Cell migration/specification is controlled by FGF8, synthesized by streak cells themselves.
Once invaginated, some cells displace the hypoblast, creating the embryonic endoderm.
Other cells come to lie between the epiblast and newly formed endoderm, forming mesoderm.
Cells remaining in the epiblast form ectoderm. Thus, the epiblast — via gastrulation — is the source of all three germ layers, which give rise to all tissues and organs of the embryo.

As more cells move between the epiblast and hypoblast, they spread laterally and cranially, eventually migrating beyond the disc margin to contact the extraembryonic mesoderm covering the yolk sac and amnion.
Fate map of the primitive streak/node

c: Lateral edges of the node / cranial streak

blocks.x: The prechordal plate

A thickening of the endoderm at the cranial end of the primitive streak, formed between the tip of the notochord and the oropharyngeal membrane. Mesodermal cells migrating cranially pass on each side of it. It later becomes important for induction of the forebrain. The oropharyngeal membrane at the cranial end consists of tightly adherent ectoderm and endoderm, representing the future opening of the oral cavity.

Intraembryonic mesoderm separates ectoderm from endoderm along the whole embryo except cranially (prechordal plate) and caudally (cloacal membrane, future site of the anus). The primitive streak regresses and disappears by the end of week 4.
Formation & functions of the notochord

Cells migrating internally through the primitive node cranially in the midline form the notochordal process, limited by the primitive pit and prechordal plate. It fuses transiently with endoderm to form the notochordal plate; as the hypoblast is replaced by endoderm, notochordal plate cells proliferate and detach to form the solid notochord, underlying the neural tube.

items: Forms a midline axis, determining the antero-posterior axis and future vertebral column site
Serves as the basis of the axial skeleton
Induces formation of the neural tube, ventral (motor) region of brain/spinal cord, and the sclerotome portion of somites (future vertebrae)
Disappears as vertebral bodies develop, but persists as the nucleus pulposus and the apical ligament of the dens of C2; remnants may give rise to chordomas

blocks.x: Differentiation of intraembryonic mesoderm

c: Somitomeres → somites → sclerotome (vertebrae, ribs, skull base) and dermomyotome (myotome = skeletal muscle; dermatome = dermis)

Splits into somatic (body wall, limb CT, sternum) and splanchnic (gut wall smooth muscle, vascular tunica media, cardiac muscle) layers, separated by the intraembryonic coelom (pericardial, pleural, peritoneal cavities)

blocks.x: Somites appear in cranio-caudal sequence between days 20–30; there are 42–44 pairs (4 occipital, 8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral, 8–10 coccygeal) — the number of somites is a useful index of embryonic age. The myotome's small dorsal epaxial division forms back muscles (innervated by dorsal rami); the larger ventral hypaxial division forms limb and body wall muscles (innervated by ventral rami).
Neurulation & the neural crest

The process by which the neural plate forms the neural tube (the early brain and spine), spanning day 18 to day 28. The notochord induces overlying ectoderm to become neuroectoderm and form the neural plate by day 18. Lateral edges elevate to form neural folds, creating a neural groove; by the end of week 3, folds fuse in the midline (beginning in the cervical region, 5th somite, proceeding cranially and caudally) to form the cylindrical neural tube. The anterior neuropore closes on day 25; the posterior neuropore closes on day 28, completing neurulation.

As neural folds fuse, cells at the tips of the folds — neural crest cells — do not join the neural tube but break away from the neuroectoderm, first remaining in the midline, then forming two dorsolateral clusters, one on either side of the neural tube.

Fate of the neural tube: the enlarged rostral part becomes the adult brain; the elongated caudal part becomes the adult spinal cord; its lumen gives rise to the ventricular system of the brain and the central canal of the spinal cord.
Clinical correlates — teratogenesis & neural tube defects

The start of week 3 is highly sensitive to teratogenic insult. High-dose alcohol exposure at this stage can kill cells in the anterior midline, causing holoprosencephaly (small forebrain, fused lateral ventricles, hypotelorism). Because this occurs ~4 weeks after the last menses, a woman may not yet recognize she is pregnant.

Insufficient mesoderm forms in the caudal-most embryo, affecting the lower limbs, urogenital system, and lumbosacral vertebrae — producing limb hypoplasia/fusion, vertebral abnormalities, renal agenesis, and imperforate anus. Associated with maternal diabetes ("mermaid syndrome").

c: Failure of anterior neuropore closure; most of the brain fails to form
Failure of closure anywhere from the cervical region caudally; most common site is lumbosacral
Failure of closure of the entire neural tube, cranial to caudal
Persistent primitive streak remnants in the sacrococcygeal region; most common newborn tumor, contains tissue from all 3 germ layers

blocks.x: 50–70% of neural tube defects are preventable with 400 µg daily folic acid. Other implicated factors: valproic acid, maternal diabetes, hyperthermia, retinoic acid excess. Elevated maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein is associated with NTDs, tested at 16–18 weeks.

The extraembryonic (fetal) membranes develop from the zygote but form no part of the embryo proper — they include the chorion, amnion, yolk sac, allantois, and umbilical cord. The placenta is the organ that facilitates nutrient and gas exchange between maternal and fetal compartments.

blocks.cap: Diagram of a placentome cross-section showing the umbilical cord, chorionic plate, stem villi carrying artery and vein branches, anchoring villi, and the basal plate

Diagram comparing the placental membrane structure before and after the 4th month, showing villous capillary, capillary endothelium, basement membranes, cytotrophoblast, syncytiotrophoblast, and intervillous space

blocks.x: Development of the villi
By the beginning of week 3, the trophoblast shows villous structures — cellular columns of cytotrophoblast surrounded by syncytium.
Mesodermal cells penetrate the core of primary villi and grow toward the decidua.

By the end of week 3, mesodermal core cells differentiate into blood cells and small vessels, forming the villous capillary system. These capillaries contact vessels in the chorionic plate and connecting stalk, then the intraembryonic circulation — so when the heart begins beating in week 4, the villous system can already supply nutrients and oxygen.

Cytotrophoblastic cells penetrate the syncytium until reaching the maternal endometrium, forming a thin outer cytotrophoblast shell that attaches the chorionic sac to the endometrium. Villi from the chorionic plate to the decidua basalis are stem (anchoring) villi; those branching from their sides are free (terminal) villi, the sites of exchange.
Fetal vs. maternal components
Develops from the chorionic plate (chorion frondosum) — trophoblast plus extraembryonic mesoderm.
Develops from the endometrium (decidua basalis) — the endometrium of a pregnant uterus is called the decidua.

c: Where the chorion frondosum attaches; forms the maternal part of the placenta
Surrounds the embryo, separating it from the uterine cavity; villi here regress into the smooth chorion laeve
The rest of the decidua; later fuses with the capsularis as the uterine cavity is obliterated

blocks.x: Maternal circulation to the placenta

Maternal blood is delivered via spiral arteries. Cytotrophoblast cells undergo endovascular invasion, replacing maternal endothelial cells to create hybrid vessels — an epithelial-to-endothelial transition that converts spiral arteries from small, high-resistance vessels into larger, low-resistance ones, supplying increased blood to the intervillous spaces.

Decidual septa project into (but don't reach) the chorionic plate, dividing the placenta into 15–20 compartments called cotyledons, while still allowing maternal blood to flow between them. The functional unit is the placentome (placental lobe) — about 50–100 exist, each a villous tree perfused by one spiral artery.
The placental membrane (barrier)

From fetal side to maternal side, before 20 weeks: capillary endothelium of fetal capillaries → connective tissue of the villus → cytotrophoblast → syncytiotrophoblast. From the 4th month, these layers thin dramatically (cytotrophoblast disappears, syncytiotrophoblast becomes very thin) to facilitate exchange. The barrier does not exclude alcohol, nicotine, viruses, drugs, exogenous hormones, or heavy metals.
Functions & features of the full-term placenta

items: Exchange of gases and metabolites between maternal and fetal circulation
Transfer of passive antibodies (e.g., diphtheria, smallpox, measles immunity)
Major endocrine organ: progesterone, estrogen, hCG, human chorionic somatomammotropin (hCS/hPL), relaxin, leptin, placental growth hormone
Discoid shape, 500–600 g, 15–20 cm diameter, 2–3 cm thick
Occupies 25–30% of the uterine surface
Maternal surface: cotyledons, cobblestone appearance, dull red
Fetal surface: smooth, shiny amnion overlying the chorion, umbilical cord attached near center

blocks.x: Clinical correlates — abnormal placentation

c: Abnormal placentation near/covering the internal cervical os; painless bleeding; classified low-lying, marginal, partial, or complete
Premature separation of the placenta after 24 weeks but before delivery; bleeding into the decidua basalis; risk of DIC, hemorrhage, shock
Villi adhere deeply into the uterine wall, not penetrating the myometrium
Villi penetrate deep into the myometrium
Villi penetrate through the myometrium to the perimetrium, possibly adhering to adjacent organs

blocks.x: Amnion & amniotic fluid

The amnion is a thin, transparent, tough membrane formed from amnioblasts and extraembryonic somatic mesoderm. It progressively envelops the connecting stalk and yolk sac stalk, forming the primitive umbilical cord, and fuses with the chorion to form the amniochorionic membrane.

Oligohydramnios (<400 ml late pregnancy) can result from renal agenesis or placental insufficiency, risking pulmonary hypoplasia and limb defects (e.g., club foot). Polyhydramnios (>2000 ml) is linked to maternal diabetes, CNS or GIT defects, and twinning.
Yolk sac, allantois & umbilical cord

items: Hemopoiesis until the liver forms (week 6)
Nutrient transfer in weeks 2–3
Contributes to the primitive gut
Source of primordial germ cells (from its endodermal lining)

blocks.x: Develops from the connecting stalk; full-term length 30–90 cm (avg 55 cm). Contains 2 umbilical arteries (deoxygenated blood to placenta) and 1 umbilical vein (oxygenated blood to fetus), embedded in Wharton's jelly. Postnatally, the arteries become the medial umbilical ligaments and the vein becomes the round ligament of the liver.
